objective: By the end of this lesson you can define learning, explain the learning theories, laws, domains, stages and memory models the FAA uses, and turn each one into something you actually do on the ground and in the airplane, including spotting and fixing the conditions that stall a learner's progress and using realistic distractions to teach workload management.
why: The FAA says an instructor has to know how people learn to take a pilot from memorized facts to judgment and problem solving [[25:52|AIH 3-1]]. On the CFI checkride you will be asked not just to define these ideas but to apply them to real ground and flight lessons, and to manage the risks of poor instruction, low motivation and uncorrected errors.

warmup: Think first: your learner flew ten nice touch-and-goes in a row last Tuesday. Today, a week later, the first three landings are poor. Did she learn anything last Tuesday? What would you change about how that lesson was built?

key_terms.def: A change in the learner's behavior that results from experience. The behavior can be physical, intellectual or attitudinal [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
A theory that explains behavior entirely as observable, measurable responses to stimuli, shaped by reinforcement from someone other than the learner [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].
A theory focused on what goes on inside the mind: knowing, perceiving, problem solving and decision making [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].
Analysis, synthesis and evaluation, the top three levels of Bloom's Taxonomy. In aviation HOTS is commonly called aeronautical decision-making (ADM) [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].
Grouping perceptions into meaningful wholes, such as seeing how power, pitch, rpm and airspeed all affect each other [[25:60|AIH 3-9]].
The law of learning that says what is learned first makes a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
The level of learning where the learner can link what was taught with other blocks of learning. It should be the goal of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].
The automatic response stage of a skill: fast and smooth, with little deliberate attention [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].
A period after early fast progress when performance levels off. It is normal and does not mean learning has stopped [[25:76|AIH 3-25]] [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].
Practice that mixes different skills through the session. It looks worse during practice but gives better retention [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].
A slip is an error of action: you planned one thing and did another. A mistake is an error of thought: you planned the wrong thing and did it [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].
The ability to apply knowledge or procedures learned in one context to new contexts [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

chunks.title: What learning is, and how it behaves

body.p: The AIH gives several definitions of learning, and they say much the same thing [[25:53|AIH 3-2]]:

bullets: A change in the learner's behavior as a result of experience. The behavior can be physical and easy to see, or it can be intellectual or attitudinal [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
The process by which experience brings about a relatively permanent change in behavior [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
Gaining knowledge or skills, or developing a behavior, through study, instruction or experience [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
A relatively permanent change in cognition (thinking) that comes from experience and directly affects behavior [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].

body.p: The common thread is experience causing a lasting change. So if learning is a change in behavior from experience, instruction has to be the careful, planned creation of the experiences that cause it [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]. An effective instructor understands the subject, the learner, the learning process and how they connect, and builds the learner's self-esteem and confidence along the way [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].
Characteristics of learning. Psychologists agree on several. To be effective, a learning situation should be purposeful, based on experience, multifaceted and active [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]:

head: Characteristic
What it means
What you do as the CFI
rows: Learning is purposeful
Each learner sees a lesson through their own goals and past experience, and learns from anything that moves those goals forward [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]
Find out why the learner is training and relate each new lesson to that goal [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]
Learning is a result of experience
The learner can only learn from personal experience. You cannot do it for them, and two people at the same event learn different things [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]
Give real experiences. Judgment comes only from experiences that require judgment on realistic problems [[25:70|AIH 3-19]]
Learning is multifaceted
Verbal, conceptual, perceptual, emotional and problem-solving learning happen at once. Learners also pick up incidental learning, such as attitudes about aviation, good or bad [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]
Watch the attitudes you model. They teach even when they are not in the lesson plan [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]
Learning is an active process
Learners do not soak up knowledge like a sponge. Being in the airplane, or quoting the right answer word for word, does not prove they can apply it [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]
Make learners react and respond, outwardly or inwardly, with questions, tasks and decisions [[25:71|AIH 3-20]]

callout.text: Application: after each lesson, ask yourself what this learner can now do that they could not do before. The definitions above say that is the only real evidence of learning [[25:53|AIH 3-2]].

check.q: A learner can recite the five steps of a level turn word for word. Does that show she can make a good turn?
check.a: No. Repeating something back is rote learning, the lowest level, and it does not mean she understands or can apply it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Quoting the correct answer verbatim is not proof she can apply it [[25:71|AIH 3-20]].

chunks.title: Learning theory: behaviorism and cognitive theory

body.p: Learning theory is a body of principles that explains how people acquire skills, knowledge and attitudes [[25:53|AIH 3-2]]. The AIH names classical conditioning, operant conditioning and social learning as primary learning theories [[25:53|AIH 3-2]]: classical conditioning is Pavlov's dog, operant conditioning links behavior to its consequences, and social learning is learning by watching and imitating others [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. Modern theories grew out of two concepts: behaviorism and cognitive theory [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

head: Theory
Core idea
In ground and flight instruction
rows: Behaviorism

Behavior is explained entirely by observable, measurable responses to stimuli and can be predicted from past rewards and punishments (the 'carrot and stick' approach). Today it stresses positive reinforcement of a behavior by someone other than the learner who shapes what is learned [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]

In aviation training the instructor provides the reinforcement [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. Praise a correct action, such as a stable approach, right away. The AIH notes behaviorism is now used more to break unwanted habits than to teach, because learning is more complex than stimulus and response [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]
Cognitive theory

Focuses on what goes on inside the mind: knowing, perceiving, problem solving, decision making and awareness. Learning is a change in how the learner thinks, understands or feels, not just a change in behavior [[25:55|AIH 3-4]]
Build on what the learner already knows, ask why and how, and give problems and decisions to work through [[25:55|AIH 3-4]] [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]

body.p: Cognitive theory has several branches you will use as a CFI:

bullets: Dewey, reflective thought: learning improves when it comes from reflection, which leads the learner from the unclear to the clear [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

Piaget: new situations create tension between old ideas (assimilation) and changing them (accommodation). People build cognitive skills by actively interacting with the world, a basic premise of scenario-based training [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

Bruner: teach from the known to the unknown and from the concrete to the abstract. His spiral curriculum revisits basic ideas again and again in more advanced ways [[25:55|AIH 3-4]], for example returning to aerodynamics on every flight lesson [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].
Bloom: the Taxonomy of the Cognitive Domain, six levels from simplest to most complex: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].
Information processing theory: the brain works like a computer that encodes, keeps and retrieves information, and lets routine actions such as rudder in a turn go unnoticed [[25:56|AIH 3-5]].
Constructivism: learners actively build knowledge from their own experience, with an experienced teacher guiding them [[25:56|AIH 3-5]] [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].

body.p: Higher order thinking skills (HOTS) are the last three Bloom levels: analysis, synthesis and evaluation. In aviation they are commonly called ADM, and the absence of HOTS is a common thread in accidents [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. Teach them from simple to complex and concrete to abstract, inside real subject matter, and in every training program, not only the first one [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].

callout.text: No single theory wins. The AIH ends the chapter by saying no one learning theory fits every situation and learner, so aviation instruction should use a combination [[25:93|AIH 3-42]].

check.q: Which learning-theory idea is called a basic premise of scenario-based training?
check.a: Piaget's conclusion that humans develop cognitive skills through active interaction with the world [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

body.p: All learning starts with perceptions, sent to the brain by the five senses, and learning is fastest when information arrives through more than one sense [[25:58|AIH 3-7]]. The AIH figure credits sight with most of it [[25:58|AIH 3-7]].

Perception is more than sensing. The person gives the sensation a meaning. A beginner is flooded by stimuli and often focuses on meaningless things, so early on you direct the learner's perceptions to what matters [[25:58|AIH 3-7]]. Five factors affect perception [[25:58|AIH 3-7]]:

head: Factor
Effect
Teaching angle
rows: Physical organism
The senses a pilot needs to see, hear, feel and respond in the air [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
A sick or tired learner perceives less (see the risk chunk) [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Goals and values
Every experience is colored by the learner's beliefs and values [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Knowing a learner's values helps you predict how they will read your instructions [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Self-concept
A negative self-image puts up psychological barriers to perceiving; a positive one makes the learner receptive [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Build a favorable self-concept with early success [[25:59|AIH 3-8]] [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]
Time and opportunity
Perceiving takes time and the right sequence. Stall recovery cannot really be learned before some normal flight experience [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Plan the syllabus so there is time to relate new sensations to earlier ones [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Element of threat
Fear narrows the perceptual field, like a learner staring at the altimeter in her first steep turns [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Never teach by threat. If a situation feels overwhelming to the learner, a threat exists [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]

body.p: Insight is grouping perceptions into meaningful wholes. In a fixed-pitch airplane, rpm changes with throttle but also with pitch attitude, so power, rpm, airspeed and attitude are all linked; seeing that link is insight [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. Insight comes eventually even without instruction, but instruction speeds it up by pointing out relationships as they happen [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. Keys: point out relationships, keep the setting secure and nonthreatening, and help the learner keep a favorable self-concept [[25:60|AIH 3-9]].

Acquiring knowledge. Here knowledge means information the learner is aware of and can put into words, such as fuel capacity or how to do a weight and balance [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]. It grows in three phases [[25:60|AIH 3-9]]:

bullets: Memorization: facts and steps. It gets the learner started quickly but fails when a question goes past the memorized facts, like whether an altimeter set too high or too low is worse in the mountains [[25:60|AIH 3-9]].

Understanding: organizing facts into a mental model of how something works, such as why the mixture is leaned as air gets less dense with altitude [[25:60|AIH 3-9]] [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. A learner who understands why steps exist can rebuild a forgotten procedure [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].
Application: using the knowledge to solve problems and make decisions [[25:61|AIH 3-10]].

body.p: Two tools organize knowledge. Concept learning groups things that share attributes into categories that get revised when exceptions show up [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. A schema is a mental framework built from repeated patterns. It is why an experienced pilot catches the key items of a long clearance while a beginner remembers 'the' and 'and' [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. Schemas can also make it hard to keep new information that does not fit them [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

callout.text: To help learners acquire knowledge, the AIH says: have them recite or practice it, ask questions that probe understanding, give problems and decisions, test the limits of what they know, show the benefit of understanding, and introduce new topics as they support the lesson objectives [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].

check.q: In her first steep turns a learner stares at the altimeter and misses the outside picture. Which factor of perception is at work?
check.a: The element of threat. Fear narrows the perceptual field to the thing causing it [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

body.p: E. L. Thorndike set down three laws of learning: readiness, exercise and effect. Three more were added later: primacy, intensity and recency [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

head: Law
What it says
How a CFI uses it
rows: Readiness
The learner's basic needs must be met, and they must want to learn and have the needed knowledge and skill [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. Learners learn best when they see a clear reason [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]

Give clear objectives, relate each topic to them, and teach in a logical order that leaves a need for the next topic [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Use teachable moments, like deer crossing the runway on final to stress go-around readiness [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]
Effect
Behaviors that lead to satisfying outcomes tend to be repeated; unpleasant outcomes make them less likely [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]
Set up success. Teaching landings on the first flight leaves a learner frustrated [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. In the debrief, praise real progress before areas to improve [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Exercise
Practice strengthens the connection and disuse weakens it: use it or lose it [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Practice skills inside real-world applications [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Primacy
What is learned first makes a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Teach it right the first time and make the first experience positive and correct [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Intensity
Immediate, exciting or dramatic learning tied to a real situation teaches more than a routine one [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Use realistic scenarios; they work for maneuvers, tasks and single-pilot resource management [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Recency
Things most recently learned are best remembered [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]
Summarize key points at the end of each lesson and debrief, and train close to the time of the real scenario [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]

callout.text: Application memory aid: Thorndike's original three are the three R-E-E words, Readiness, Exercise, Effect. The three added later run P-I-R: Primacy, Intensity, Recency [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

body.p: Readiness and human needs. The AIH says the order of needs in Maslow's hierarchy matters little; what matters is that you check most needs are met (law of readiness) with a pre-assessment that the learner is physically and mentally ready to learn [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

check.q: Which law is the reason to insist on correct checklist use the very first time you teach it?
check.a: Primacy. What is learned first creates a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]], and correct habits are easier to build than faulty ones are to fix [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

body.p: Bloom sorted learning into three domains: cognitive (thinking), affective (feeling) and psychomotor (doing) [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

Cognitive. The domain of facts, concepts and intellectual skills, with six levels from recalling facts to evaluation [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. For aviation the AIH uses four practical learning levels: rote, understanding, application and correlation [[25:65|AIH 3-14]].

head: Level
What the learner can do
Turn-entry example
rows: Rote
Repeat what was taught without understanding or applying it [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Recites the five steps of a level turn [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Understanding
Put two or more concepts together and describe or explain [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Knows why each step matters after learning what the controls do [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Application
Use what was learned; reached after demonstration and practice to consistency [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Enters turns well on her own. Stopping here is piecemeal instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Correlation
Associate the element with other blocks of learning; this should be the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Uses turn entries correctly while flying the traffic pattern [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]

body.p: Above these sit the HOTS levels of analysis, synthesis and evaluation [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Ground school, reading and briefings usually reach the first three levels; the highest ones are reached through SBT [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

Affective. The learner's emotions toward learning: feelings, values, enthusiasm, motivation and attitudes, including attitude toward safety and risk [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. It has five levels: awareness, response, value, organizing and integration, ending when the learner internalizes the value [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. It is harder to measure, but motivation and enthusiasm matter in all learning [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

Psychomotor. Physical skill: movement, coordination and motor skills, built by repetitive practice and measured by speed, precision, distance and technique [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. The practical levels for aviation are observation, imitation, practice and habit [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. The learner first watches an expert, then copies under your eye, then repeats it (even solo touch-and-goes), and reaches habit when they can do it in twice the time the instructor or an expert takes [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].

callout.text: Write objectives with action verbs for the domain you are aiming at. The AIH says these verbs are performance-based objectives and can be tied to the ACS [[25:69|AIH 3-18]].

check.q: A learner now does the full passenger briefing even when you are not watching, because she believes it matters. Which domain is that?
check.a: The affective domain, near its top level, where she has organized the value into her own beliefs and internalized it [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

body.p: Skill knowledge shows up in doing: motor or mental skills the learner is usually not aware of and cannot put into words, like riding a bicycle. You only see it by watching performance, and it is acquired slowly through practice [[25:74|AIH 3-23]].
Stages. The AIH names three stages of skill acquisition: cognitive, associative and automatic response. You need to recognize each one to judge progress [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

head: Stage
What you see
What you do
rows: Cognitive
The learner follows memorized steps, may fixate on one part, and is often unaware of progress. Distractions make performance fall apart or stop [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Give a clear, step-by-step demonstration so they have a model [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Associative
The learner links steps to results, checks progress and adjusts. It still takes deliberate attention but distractions are handled better [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Let them practice. Short, specific comments now mean more than a long explanation did before they started [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Automatic response
Fast and smooth, with few and small corrections. The learner can talk while flying and may not be able to explain the steps: 'I have developed a feel for it' [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Add other tasks and realistic distractions [[25:75|AIH 3-24]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]

body.p: Knowledge of results. Learners need to know their progress, as much when they are right as when they are wrong. Tell them as soon after the performance as possible and do not let them practice mistakes, because unlearning a mistake is harder than learning it right the first time [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. One way: repeat the demonstration and show the standard their performance should meet [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

How to develop skills. Every theory agrees progress depends on repeated practice. Early trials are slow and uncoordinated, and each trial gives clues for the next [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. The power law of practice says speed of performance improves as a power of the number of trials: fast gains at first, slower gains later [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].

Learning plateaus. After the early fast gains the curve may level off for a long time [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. A plateau may mean the learner hit capability limits, is consolidating, has lost interest, or needs a better method; it does not mean learning has stopped, and in motor skills it is normal [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Tell the learner ahead of time that plateaus are normal and temporary, move to a different part of the syllabus for a while, and explain the lesson, its reason and how it applies better [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Know that you can cause a plateau by over-practice [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

callout.text: Plateaus are a common source of frustration, discouragement and lower motivation [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. If you keep drilling the same maneuver, you may be the cause [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

check.q: A learner lands well when you stay quiet, but a radio question on short final makes the landing fall apart. Which stage is she probably in?
check.a: The cognitive stage. The skill takes all her attention, and distractions cause performance to deteriorate or stop [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

chunks.title: Types of practice, and evaluation versus critique

body.p: How practice is structured has a big effect on how well people keep what they learn. There are three types: deliberate, blocked and random [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

head: Type
What it is
Result
rows: Deliberate
Practice aimed at a goal: specific areas, with specific feedback on the gap between actual and goal performance [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]
Builds a skill toward automatic. Avoid distractions and keep feedback brief and explicit [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]
Blocked
The same drill over and over until it is automatic, like repeated crosswind landings [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Better short-term performance but poorer long-term learning; it fools the learner and the instructor [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Random
Different skills mixed through the session [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Better retention. It scores worse during practice but better on a test the next day [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]

body.p: How much practice: a beginner reaches a point where more practice is useless or harmful, errors rise and motivation drops. More experienced learners profit from longer periods [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Practicing the same skill in different settings, such as the airplane, then a model on the ground, then a video of landings to critique, adds new perceptions and insight [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

Overlearning is practice past initial proficiency. It can make work faster, but it can also turn a checklist into a recitation separated from the thinking it should trigger. In one study pilots and instructors did poorly on weight and balance charts from an unfamiliar airplane [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

Evaluation versus critique. In the early stages of skill learning, practical suggestions help more than a grade [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. Early evaluation is mostly teacher oriented: it checks teaching effectiveness, predicts outcomes and finds problem areas and the learner's strengths and weaknesses, which you need before you can give constructive criticism [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. A critique is watching the practice and giving constructive feedback to remove errors, with praise for what went well. Letting the learner critique their own performance makes it learner-centered [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

head: Evaluation
Critique
rows: Main purpose
Measure progress and check your own teaching [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Improve the performance with practical suggestions [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Timing
Periodic. Formal assessments are documented, like a quiz or written exam [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]
Right after the performance, while details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Content
Strengths and weaknesses to plan the next step [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Good and bad parts, how they relate and the whole performance; never just a chance to be overly critical [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]

body.p: Critique formats in the AIH: instructor/learner, learner-led, small group, by another learner, self-critique and written. In every one, the instructor stays in control and corrects wrong impressions [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

callout.text: Learners can drift away from the intended method at any stage of skill acquisition, so keep watching even good learners [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

check.q: After eight touch-and-goes in a row the landings looked great, but a week later they are poor again. What practice structure probably caused it?
check.a: Blocked practice: good short-term performance but poorer long-term learning. Mix the skills with random practice for better retention [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

body.p: SBT is a training system that uses a structured script of real-world scenarios to meet flight training objectives in an operational environment [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. It sits at the heart of HOTS: it ties new information to old, presents it in a realistic context and gives realistic decision practice [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].

Adapt each scenario to the aircraft and its likely flight environment, require real-time decisions, and have the learner plan and lead it, except for the first flight or two [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. Used well, the learner forms possible solutions, evaluates them, decides, judges the decision and reflects on the thinking behind it [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].
A good scenario:

bullets: Has clear objectives, is tailored to the learner and uses the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].
Is not a test, has no single correct answer and no obvious answer [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].
Engages all three learning domains and is interactive [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].
Does not promote errors, promotes situational awareness and decision making, and requires time-pressured decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

body.p: Build it in layers. System safety training runs in three phases: stick-and-rudder skills first, then the hazards and risks (much of it on the ground, with no added flight time), then a complex scenario, such as a sick passenger forcing a diversion to a short runway where the flaps then fail [[25:30|AIH 1-26]] [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Before the flight, the instructor and learner set the scenario destination, desired outcomes, desired level of performance and possible inflight changes, and you decide in advance which outcomes are good and which are poor [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

Grow one scenario as the learner grows. Bill used a low-fuel scenario first in the classroom, then near the home airport, then at another airport, then on a cross-country to a hard-to-spot remote field, and finally with eight airports in view [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. There is no list of canned scenarios; build each one from what the learner needs next and what the local area offers [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

callout.text: Once the learner starts making the decisions, step back into the role of mentor or learning facilitator [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. After the flight, use collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment first, then compare it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: What four things should the instructor and learner set before an SBT flight?
check.a: The scenario destination(s), the desired learning outcome(s), the desired level of learner performance and possible inflight scenario changes [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

body.p: People generally cannot look at two things at once or follow two conversations; sharp central vision covers only a few degrees [[25:80|AIH 3-29]]. What looks like multitasking is really attention switching, and the danger is deferring a task and then forgetting it [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

head: Problem
What it is
Teaching angle
rows: Distraction
An unexpected event that pulls attention away for a moment. The learner decides whether to act on it or go back to the task [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Teach that decision: deal with it, or let it go and return to the task [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Interruption
The learner chooses to stop one task to do another. A big source of errors, such as going back to a checklist at the wrong item [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Have learners build a procedure for interruptions [[25:81|AIH 3-30]], like the trained pilot who mentally bookmarks her place [[25:52|AIH 3-1]]
Fixation
Absorbed in one task while others slide, like a new instrument pilot locked on one gauge. Often a sign the task needs more practice by itself [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Point it out when it happens [[25:83|AIH 3-32]] and give more isolated practice [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Inattention
Failing to attend to an important task, from fixation or from boredom. Humans are poor passive monitors, and get worse as systems become more reliable [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Alert the learner to it and build habits that keep attention focused [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]

body.p: Spot it by following the learner's eyes. A long stare at one instrument suggests fixation; never looking at the engine gauges suggests inattention. But looking is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Sequence matters. Before asking for several tasks at once, make sure each one can be done reasonably well alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Do not confuse distractions during early skill learning, which hurt, with the planned use of distractions to teach attention management once skills are partly mastered [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

Realistic distractions. NTSB data show most stall/spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted from flying; the real danger was inadvertent stalls caused by distractions in routine flight, not intentional stall practice [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The most effective training simulates those scenarios by creating distractions while the learner practices certain maneuvers, and you teach the learner to divide attention between the distraction and aircraft control [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. AIH examples [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]:

bullets: Drop a pencil and ask the learner to pick it up.
Ask for a heading to an airport using a chart, or to compute true airspeed with a flight computer.
Ask the learner to reset the clock or read the outside air temperature.
Ask the learner to get something from the back seat.
Ask the learner to identify terrain, objects, or a field suitable for a forced landing.
Have the learner climb 200 feet and level off, then descend 200 feet and level off, or reverse course after a series of S-turns.

body.p: Managing a workload. Raise the workload gradually while you watch how the learner handles it, and teach them to recognize overload and then stop, think, slow down and prioritize, handing tasks to a passenger, an autopilot or ATC [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. The first effect of high workload is that the pilot may be working harder but getting less done [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Have learners practice automation changes in scenarios so a programming change does not become a major distraction [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

callout.text: Teach the learner to take charge: a pilot in command must know when to tell any passenger, even an examiner, that their actions are interfering with safe flight [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Model a sterile flight deck yourself during critical phases [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Why not drop the pencil while a learner is flying her very first steep turns?
check.a: In the cognitive stage the skill takes all her attention, so distractions make performance fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Each task should be done reasonably well alone before you add others [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

chunks.title: Errors, and recognizing and correcting them

body.p: Errors are a natural part of human performance for beginners and experts alike; believing you can eliminate them is the biggest error of all [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. There are two kinds [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]:

head: Kind
What it is
Example
rows: Slip

An error of action: you plan one thing and do another. Forms include leaving a step out, confusing two similar things, doing a changed routine the old way, and hurrying (the speed-accuracy tradeoff) [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]
Assigned runway 12 after many days on 30, the learner enters the pattern for 30 out of habit [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]
Mistake
An error of thought: you plan the wrong thing and do it successfully, often from a gap or misconception [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]
An expert ignores a real traffic alert because he has learned to ignore nuisance alerts near home [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]

body.p: Ways to reduce errors [[25:84|AIH 3-33]] [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]:

bullets: Learning and practicing: more knowledge and skill means fewer and smaller errors [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].
Taking time: work at a comfortable pace [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].
Checking for errors: look actively for evidence of them [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].
Using reminders: checklists, heading bugs and notepads [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].
Developing routines: standard procedures for routine tasks [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].
Raising awareness when errors are likely, such as a change in routine, time pressure, fatigue or lack of recent practice [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

body.p: Error recovery and learning from error. Practice recovering from common or serious errors, like the lost procedure [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. When an error happens, ask the learner why it happened and what would prevent it, but do not let them practice the wrong thing [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. Watch for the human habit of explaining errors away and for hindsight bias [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

Recognizing and correcting learner errors. Correction does not mean taking over the moment a mistake is made. Safety permitting, let the learner go part way into it and find the way out, because a learner who seldom corrects an error has trouble learning the maneuver [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. If you suspect a learner does a maneuver right without understanding it, have them vary it, combine it with other operations or apply it to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. In the learner tells, learner does step, having the learner talk through the maneuver shows you whether an error comes from a misconception or simply a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Safety sets the limit. Never let a learner exceed your own limits; when you take over, say 'I have the flight controls' and make sure the learner lets go, because anxious learners can be incredibly strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Your learner means to select ground control but dials in the tower frequency she used last flight. Slip or mistake, and what helps?
check.a: A slip, an error of action from habit in a changed routine [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. Reminders, standard routines and checking her work help reduce it [[25:84|AIH 3-33]] [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

body.p: Memory is the ability to encode, store and retrieve information. A widely accepted model has three parts: sensory memory, short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM) [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

Sensory memory takes in stimuli from the environment and, within seconds, throws out what seems unimportant and passes what matters to STM. That preset filter is called precoding, as when a fire alarm gets instant attention [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Dramatic input that hits more than one sense is more likely to make an impression [[25:87|AIH 3-36]].

Short-Term Memory (STM) and Long-Term Memory (LTM). STM holds information for roughly 30 seconds and about seven chunks. Coding takes 5 to 10 seconds, and if it is interrupted the information is easily lost [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Rehearsal and chunking help, and recoding, relating new information to what is already known, is where real learning begins [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. LTM is relatively permanent with unlimited capacity. Information reaches it when it has significance (like a first solo), is repeated, or is attached to something significant [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. LTM is a reconstruction, not a perfect recording [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. It is organized in schemas, so activate them with a short review of the last lesson before new material [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].
How usage affects memory. Recall depends mainly on how often (frequency) and how recently (recency) the knowledge has been used [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]:

head: Usage pattern
What it is
Recall and fix
rows: Frequency and recency
Used a lot before and still used now [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]
Retrieved easily and quickly; the ideal [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]
Frequency only
Used a lot in the past but not lately [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]
Slow or no recall; add recent practice to refresh it [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]
Recency only
Just learned [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]
Very easy to forget, like throw-away facts; needs regular rehearsal to build frequency [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]

body.p: Forgetting usually means a failure to retrieve: the information is still somewhere in LTM but cannot be reached [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. The theories [[25:88|AIH 3-37]] [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]:

bullets: Retrieval failure: the tip-of-the-tongue problem, plus information never stored well in the first place (failure to store) [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].
Fading: information not used for a long time fades or decays [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].
Interference: newer or similar learning overshadows the old; similar material interferes most, and material not well learned suffers most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].
Repression or suppression: a memory is pushed out of reach to avoid unpleasant feelings; repression is unconscious, suppression conscious [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].

callout.text: Application: because interrupted coding in STM is easily lost [[25:87|AIH 3-36]], do not start talking while a learner is copying a clearance or setting up an approach.

check.q: A pilot practiced stalls every week in training two years ago and has not flown one since. Which usage pattern is this, and what fixes it?
check.a: Frequency only. The knowledge is likely to come back slowly or not at all until recent practice refreshes it [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

body.p: Retention of learning. Forgotten material is usually still there but unavailable, so your job is to make sure learning can be recalled [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Teach thoroughly and with meaning; rote learning is superficial and not easily kept [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Five principles help [[25:89|AIH 3-38]] [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]:

bullets: Praise stimulates remembering; negativism makes recall less likely [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].
Recall is promoted by association; unique, disconnected facts tend to be forgotten [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].
Favorable attitudes aid retention: people remember what they want to know [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].
Learning with all senses is most effective [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].
Meaningful repetition aids recall, but practice gives a chance to learn without causing it; three or four repetitions give the most effect [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

body.p: In a lecture, retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes until the last 5 to 10 minutes, and passive listeners keep roughly five percent over 24 hours [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]. Mnemonics such as acronyms, acrostics (ANDS for a compass error), rhymes and chaining help recall information in order [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]. Shorter, regularly spaced study beats cramming, and even writing study questions improves recall [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. A certificate does not stop forgetting; only continued practice keeps the skill [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

Transfer of learning is the ability to apply knowledge or procedures learned in one context to new ones; practicing under a variety of conditions gives positive transfer [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]. Near transfer goes to closely related settings, far transfer to different settings and new problems with a shared structure, and generativity means the learner comes up with new solutions alone [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

head: Transfer
Example from the AIH
rows: Positive: learning skill A helps skill B
Slow flight practice helps short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]
Negative: learning skill A hinders skill B
Airplane approach practice may hinder learning helicopter approaches [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]

body.p: To help transfer [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]: plan for it as a primary objective; show learners the information applies to other situations; keep high-order standards (overlearning may be appropriate); avoid unnecessary rote learning, which does not foster transfer; give meaningful experiences that build confidence; and use materials that make relationships clear.

callout.text: Habit formation and the building block concept: insist on correct technique from the start (primacy), and base each new piece of learning on a solid foundation of old learning [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

check.q: Why does the AIH tell you to avoid unnecessary rote learning if your goal is transfer?
check.a: Because rote learning does not foster transfer; thorough understanding makes learners more likely to see how the material relates to new situations [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

chunks.title: Risks: inadequate instruction, lost motivation and other barriers

body.p: Inadequate or incomplete instruction. Learners become apathetic when they see the instructor has not prepared, or the instruction seems deficient, contradictory or insincere; nothing destroys interest faster than a poorly organized lesson [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Instruction can also be too complicated, too elementary or too general. Teach for the learner's level: a preflight lesson for a skilled maintenance technician should look different from one for a beginner [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Distracting mannerisms, untidiness, irritation or talking down to the learner lose confidence that is hard to win back [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Stopping at the application level and moving on is piecemeal instruction, usually inefficient [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Learners who believe their instruction is inadequate, or your demands unreasonable, do not learn well and lose motivation [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

Lack of learner motivation. Motivation is probably the dominant force in a learner's progress [[25:35|AIH 2-2]]. Positive motivation, the promise or achievement of rewards, works better than negative motivation such as fear [[25:35|AIH 2-2]]. Avoid negative motivation with all but the most overconfident and impulsive learners [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]. Drops are natural after the first excitement and between big events like solo, stage checks or practical tests; they show up as learners coming unprepared or acting as if training is no longer a priority [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. The AIH's instructor actions [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]:

bullets: Ask new learners about their aviation training goals.
Reward incremental successes.
Present new challenges.
Now and then remind learners of their own stated goals.
Assure them that plateaus are normal and improvement will return with effort.

body.p: Conditions that undermine the learning process, and how to correct them:

head: Condition
What you see
How to correct it
rows: Anxiety
Hesitation, freezing, or acting without thought [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Treat fears as normal. Before stalls, review the aerodynamics, then describe the sensations and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Impatience
Wants to solo or fly cross-countries before the basics are learned [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Teach one step at a time with clear goals, and move a fast learner on as soon as each goal is met [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Worry or lack of interest
Emotional upset; not ready to learn [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Make sure learners know the objective of each step and, after each lesson, how they are progressing [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Physical discomfort, illness, airsickness
Slower learning; an airsick learner cannot learn at a normal rate [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
End the flight at the first sign of airsickness; fresh air and letting them fly help [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Fatigue
Inattention, distractibility, errors in timing, neglect of secondary tasks, loss of accuracy, irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Give a break; continue only while the learner is alert and receptive [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Apathy due to inadequate instruction
Interest fades when the learner notices poor preparation [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Give well-planned, appropriate and accurate instruction [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]

callout.text: Abnormal reactions to stress, such as inappropriate laughter, sharp mood swings or severe anger at the instructor, call for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. If you suspect a serious psychological problem, have an instructor who does not know the learner fly an evaluation, then confer; withhold solo endorsements and test recommendations if the concern stands [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

check.q: What are the five instructor actions the AIH lists to keep learners working hard?
check.a: Ask about their training goals, reward incremental successes, present new challenges, remind them of their stated goals, and assure them plateaus are normal [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

body.p: These are instructor errors the AIH warns about. Each one undermines the learning process, and each one is an easy oral question on the checkride.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Teaching something too hard too early, like landings on the first flight
A frustrated learner who feels inferior [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]
Set up success first (law of effect) [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]
Stopping at the application level
Good turn entries alone, poor ones in the traffic pattern [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Teach to correlation by tying each element to other blocks [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Long explanations before the learner has tried
Confusion [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Clear demonstration, then short specific comments during practice [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Letting the learner practice mistakes
Errors become habits that are hard to unlearn [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]
Give knowledge of results right away; repeat the demonstration and show the standard [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]
Only blocked practice
Good today, poor next week [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Use random practice and scenarios [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Talking or distracting during early skill practice
Performance falls apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]
Avoid conversation during individual skill practice; add planned distractions later [[25:80|AIH 3-29]]
Over-practice
A plateau, more errors, falling motivation [[25:77|AIH 3-26]] [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]
Move to a different part of the syllabus and come back [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]
Threats or harsh critique
Narrowed perception and rejection of training [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
A nonthreatening setting; praise progress before areas to improve [[25:64|AIH 3-13]] [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]
Taking the controls at the first error
A learner who never learns to correct [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Safety permitting, let the learner go part way into the error and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

callout.text: Apply the theory out loud on the checkride. When you teach a maneuver, name the law, stage or domain behind each choice: 'I am demonstrating first because she is in the cognitive stage and needs a model' [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

check.q: You notice your learner's errors and take the controls every time, before she can react. What does the AIH say is lost?
check.a: Her chance to correct errors. It is difficult to learn a maneuver properly with few chances to correct an error, so, safety permitting, let her progress part way into the mistake [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

scenario.title: The learner who stopped improving
scenario.setup: You have just taken over Jordan, a private pilot learner with 48 hours, from an instructor who left the school. Jordan works long night shifts. His logbook shows the last three lessons were ten touch-and-goes each in the same pattern, with no notes on how they went. Jordan's landings have not improved in three weeks, he came to today's lesson without doing the assigned reading, and he says, 'Maybe I'm just not a natural.' On his last flight, the tower gave him a frequency change in the middle of the before-landing checklist, and when he went back to the list he skipped the fuel selector.

questions.q: What is most likely happening with Jordan's landing progress?
questions.a: A learning plateau. After early fast gains, progress often levels off; it is normal and does not mean learning has stopped [[25:76|AIH 3-25]] [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Over-practice can bring one on [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

questions.q: How would you restructure the landing practice?
questions.a: Three straight lessons of the same drill is blocked practice, which looks good short term but gives poorer long-term learning. Mix skills with random practice and a scenario [[25:78|AIH 3-27]], move to a different part of the syllabus for a while, and come back [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

questions.q: Jordan's comment and missed reading point to which risk, and what do you do?
questions.a: A drop in motivation [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Ask about his goals and remind him of them, reward small successes, give a new challenge and tell him plateaus are normal and temporary [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

questions.q: What kind of error was the skipped fuel selector, and how do you train against it?
questions.a: An interruption error: he suspended the checklist for the radio call and picked up at a later point [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. It is a slip, an error of action [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. Teach a procedure for interruptions and the use of reminders and routines [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

questions.q: The previous instructor wrote no notes and gave no feedback. Why does that matter?
questions.a: Learners need knowledge of results as soon after the performance as possible, and should not practice mistakes [[25:76|AIH 3-25]]. A critique belongs right after the performance, covering the good as well as the bad [[25:141|AIH 6-10]]. Missing feedback can also feel like inadequate instruction, which hurts motivation [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

questions.q: Jordan arrives straight from a night shift. What do you check first?
questions.a: Fatigue. Look for signs like inattention, errors in timing and irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Fatigue is the primary consideration in lesson length, and instruction should continue only while he is alert and receptive [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

skills.do: Apply educational theories to ground and flight instruction (ACS FI.I.B.S1). The examiner sees you plan and teach a lesson where you can name the theory, law, domain or stage behind each step and explain why it fits this learner.
skills.practice: Take one maneuver and write a one-page plan that names the level of learning you are aiming for (correlation is the goal) [[25:66|AIH 3-15]], the law of learning behind your opening [[25:62|AIH 3-11]], and how you will move from demonstration to practice [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Teach it to a friend out loud.

skills.do: Recognize and correct conditions that undermine the learning process (ACS FI.I.B.S2). The examiner describes or role-plays a learner who is anxious, impatient, tired, unmotivated or stuck on a plateau, and you name the condition and the fix.
skills.practice: Make flash cards with a symptom on one side (freezing, rushing to solo, yawning and irritable, coming unprepared) and the AIH condition and fix on the other [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:47|AIH 2-14]] [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Drill until you can answer in one sentence.

skills.do: Plan for and use techniques, including realistic distractions that teach flight students how to manage a workload (ACS FI.I.B.S3). The examiner sees you brief and use distractions only after the skill is partly mastered, while keeping the airplane safe.
skills.practice: Pick three distractions from the AIH list [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] and plan where each fits in a lesson. Practice from the right seat with a safety pilot: give the distraction, watch for fixation and inattention [[25:82|AIH 3-31]], and debrief how the workload was managed [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

quiz.q: Which learning theory says behavior is shaped by reinforcement from someone other than the learner?
quiz.why: Modern behaviorism stresses positive reinforcement by someone other than the learner who shapes what is learned; in aviation training that is the instructor [[25:54|AIH 3-3]].

options: Teaching every topic once, in a fixed order, then moving on for good
Revisiting basic ideas repeatedly and building on them in more advanced ways
Moving from abstract principles first to concrete examples later in the course
Letting the learner choose the order of topics as interest grows
quiz.why: The spiral curriculum revisits basic ideas repeatedly and builds on them in increasingly sophisticated ways [[25:55|AIH 3-4]].

quiz.q: In the AIH, what is insight?
options: The grouping of perceptions into meaningful wholes
The first impression a lesson makes
A learner's ability to recite a procedure
A sudden guess that turns out right
quiz.why: Insight involves the grouping of perceptions into meaningful wholes, and creating it is one of the instructor's major responsibilities [[25:60|AIH 3-9]].

options: A list of memorized steps a learner recites in order without understanding
A cognitive framework for organizing and interpreting information
quiz.why: A schema is the cognitive framework that helps people organize and interpret information, formed from recurring patterns [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

quiz.q: Which list gives the practical psychomotor levels for aviation training?
quiz.why: The AIH lists observation, imitation, practice and habit as the practical psychomotor levels for aviation training [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].

quiz.q: In which stage of skill acquisition might a learner say, 'I have developed a feel for it,' and be unable to list the steps?
quiz.why: At the automatic response stage the learner performs smoothly and may no longer remember or explain the individual steps [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

quiz.q: Which type of practice gives specific feedback on the gap between actual and goal performance?
quiz.why: In deliberate practice the learner works on specific areas and gets feedback that points out discrepancies between actual and goal performance [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

quiz.q: In short-term memory, what is recoding?
options: Repeating a phone number over and over until the moment it is used
Relating new information to knowledge already in memory
Discarding unimportant stimuli from the senses within a few seconds
Pushing an unpleasant memory out of reach so it cannot be recalled
quiz.why: Recoding adjusts information to the individual's experience by relating it to what is already in memory; this is when actual learning begins [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Repeating a number is rehearsal, discarding stimuli is the sensory register, and pushing memories away is repression or suppression.

quiz.q: According to interference theory, which material suffers most from interference?
quiz.why: Similar material interferes more than dissimilar material, and material not well learned suffers most from interference [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].

quiz.q: Negative motivation should be avoided with all but which learners?
options: The most anxious and easily discouraged
quiz.why: Positive motivation is essential to true learning; negative motivation should be avoided with all but the most overconfident and impulsive learners [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies turns around a point within limits but cannot plan a safe arrival at an unfamiliar nontowered airport. What does the AIH say gets her to that higher level?
options: More repetitions of turns around a point until they are perfect
A longer ground lecture on wind drift
Scenario-based training that has her plan and decide
A written test on traffic patterns
final_quiz.why: Ground school and briefings usually reach knowledge, comprehension and application; the highest levels (analysis, synthesis, evaluation) are acquired through SBT [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. Bill's arrival-planning lesson is the AIH example [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: Deer cross the runway while your learner is on final, and you use it right away to stress always being ready to go around. What is this?
options: Negative transfer from an earlier lesson
final_quiz.why: Readiness includes the teachable moment, when a learner is especially responsive; the AIH uses this exact deer example [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

final_quiz.q: During the run-up checklist the tower calls. After answering, the learner resumes the list but skips the magneto check. What happened?
options: An interruption that caused an omitted step
final_quiz.why: An interruption is when the learner suspends one task for another; a classic error is returning to a checklist at a later point and omitting steps [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

final_quiz.q: Over several flights you notice your learner's eyes never go to the engine gauges. What problem might this show?
final_quiz.why: Learners whose gaze is never directed toward engine instruments might have a problem with inattention; a long stare at one instrument suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: A learner with a simple, wrong idea of how fronts behave plans a flight that takes him into weather he did not expect, flying the plan exactly as he intended. What kind of error is this?
final_quiz.why: A mistake is an error of thought: planning the wrong thing and doing it. Overly simple understanding of weather often leads inexperienced learners into unexpected situations [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].

final_quiz.q: On a checkride an applicant knows the answer to a question but cannot bring it to mind. Which theory of forgetting fits best?
final_quiz.why: Retrieval failure is the tip-of-the-tongue inability to retrieve information the person knows [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner just learned the light-gun signals yesterday and has never used them. How vulnerable is that knowledge, and what does it need?
options: Safe, because anything learned well once is stored for good
It will move to long-term memory no matter what you do next
Very vulnerable; it needs rehearsal to build frequency
final_quiz.why: Recency-only knowledge is particularly vulnerable to being forgotten and needs a program of regular rehearsal to build its frequency [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

final_quiz.q: Practice in slow flight makes your learner's short-field landings easier to learn. What is this?
final_quiz.why: If learning skill A helps learning skill B, positive transfer occurs; slow flight helping short-field landings is the AIH example [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

final_quiz.q: A learner who passed his knowledge test last month answers regulation questions better than you, his instructor, do. What does the AIH say explains this?
options: His recent rehearsal outweighs your more frequent but less recent use
He learned by rote, and rote learning is retained longer than understanding
Instructors cannot forget material they teach often
The law of primacy: he learned the rules first
final_quiz.why: In one study learners' retention of some topics beat their instructors': recent active use and rehearsal outweighed more frequent but less recent use. An instructor's knowledge is just as vulnerable to forgetting [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. Rote learning is superficial and not easily retained [[25:89|AIH 3-38]].

final_quiz.q: You arrive late and teach a lesson you clearly have not prepared. The learner tunes out. Which barrier have you created?
options: Impatience with the pace of the lesson
final_quiz.why: Learners become apathetic when they see the instructor has made inadequate preparations; nothing destroys interest as quickly as a poorly organized lesson [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

final_quiz.q: A nervous learner is about to see his first power-off stall. What should you do first?
options: Demonstrate it without warning so he sees it fresh, with no time to worry
Review the aerodynamics, then describe the sensations and the recovery
Tell him stalls cause most fatal accidents
final_quiz.why: Introduce such maneuvers with care: review the aerodynamic principles, then describe the physical sensations and the recovery procedures; treat fears as normal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: According to the NTSB data in the AIH, what was the real danger in stall/spin accidents?
options: Intentional stall practice during dual and solo training flights
Intentional spin training, even with an instructor aboard
Inadvertent stalls caused by distractions in routine flight
final_quiz.why: Intentional practice of stalls and spins seldom resulted in accidents; the real danger was inadvertent stalls induced by distractions during routine flight [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a trait of a good training scenario?
options: It engages all three learning domains
final_quiz.why: A good scenario is not a test and will not have a single correct answer; it engages all three domains, is interactive and requires time-pressured decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

takeaways: Learning is a lasting change in behavior caused by experience, so your job is to build the right experiences.
Use a mix of theories: reinforce like a behaviorist, but build understanding and decisions like a cognitive theorist.
The six laws: readiness, exercise, effect, primacy, intensity, recency. Teach it right the first time.
Aim for correlation, not just application, and grow judgment with scenario-based training.
Skills move from cognitive to associative to automatic; give fast feedback, mix your practice, expect plateaus.
Add realistic distractions only after a skill is partly mastered, and teach the learner to manage workload.
Watch for poor instruction, low motivation, fatigue and uncorrected errors; they quietly stop learning.
cfi_notes: Expect the examiner to ask you to explain each law, domain and stage with a flight example. Prepare one airplane example for every item in this Task.

The AIH gives two psychomotor lists: Figure 3-12 shows a seven-level taxonomy (perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response, adaptation, origination), while the text and Figure 3-8 give four practical levels for aviation: observation, imitation, practice, habit [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:68|AIH 3-17]]. The text says various versions exist, so this is a choice, not an error. Teach the four, and know the seven exist if an examiner shows you the figure.

The AIH counts the demonstration-performance phases two ways. Chapter 5 lists five (explanation, demonstration, learner performance, instructor supervision, evaluation) [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]; Chapter 9 lists four because it joins learner performance with instructor supervision, which happen at the same time [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Know both and say which chapter you are using.

The chapter 9 summary says it covered 'obstacles to learning encountered during flight training' [[25:184|AIH 9-14]], but that chapter has no such section. In this edition those barriers (anxiety, impatience, worry, discomfort, fatigue, apathy) are in Chapter 2 [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

The AIH itself warns that Maslow's hierarchy has little empirical support and that the order of needs matters little [[25:38|AIH 2-5]] [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Teach readiness as a quick pre-assessment that the learner is physically and mentally ready, not as a rigid pyramid.
Learning styles: the AIH notes controversy over their scientific value [[25:71|AIH 3-20]] and its advice is to address a variety of styles in every lesson [[25:74|AIH 3-23]], not to label a learner.
'Recency' means two things in this chapter: the law of recency [[25:64|AIH 3-13]] and recency of use in memory [[25:88|AIH 3-37]]. Say which one you mean in an oral.
Use the learner tells, instructor does step to check understanding before the learner takes the controls; it lets you correct misunderstandings before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
In a debrief, let the learner self-assess first, then compare it with yours (collaborative assessment) [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. It turns a critique into learner-centered training [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].
gaps: No source gives a number for how long a lesson or practice block should be. The AIH says fatigue is the primary consideration [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] and that beginners reach a point where more practice hurts [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]; the rest is CFI judgment.
The AIH says learners should develop procedures for interruptions [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] but gives no standard method for resuming an interrupted checklist. Use your school's or the aircraft's SOP.
The affective domain is called harder to measure [[25:67|AIH 3-16]], and the sources give no tool for measuring it.
The perception percentages and the five-percent lecture retention figure are stated in the AIH without the studies behind them [[25:58|AIH 3-7]] [[25:90|AIH 3-39]]. Use them as illustrations.
The PHAK and RMH listed in the Task references say little about learning theory itself; nearly all of this Task comes from the AIH, with workload and automation points from PHAK 2-24 and RMH 7-2.

activities.title: Numbers behind the learning process
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Figure 3-5: sight gives 75 percent and hearing 13 percent of perception. What percent do sight and hearing give together?
items.why: 75 + 13 = 88 percent, which matches the figure caption. Teach with more than one sense [[25:58|AIH 3-7]].

items.q: NTSB data in the AIH: 60 percent of stall/spin accidents occurred during takeoff and landing. Out of 50 stall/spin accidents, how many would that be?
items.why: 0.60 x 50 = 30. Most stall/spin accidents came when attention was diverted, which is why you train with realistic distractions [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

items.q: You fly the after-landing flow in 45 seconds. Within how many seconds must your learner do it to reach the psychomotor habit level?
items.why: Habit is reached when the learner can do the skill in twice the time the instructor or an expert takes: 2 x 45 = 90 seconds [[25:68|AIH 3-17]].

items.q: Passive lecture listeners keep roughly five percent over 24 hours. Your ground lecture covers 40 key facts. About how many will a passive listener still have tomorrow?
items.why: 0.05 x 40 = 2 facts. Active learners keep much more, so make learners respond [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

items.q: Retention drops after the first 10 to 15 minutes of a lesson and recovers only in the last 5 to 10 minutes. In a 60-minute lecture, at least how many minutes fall in the low-retention middle?
items.why: Shortest low stretch uses the longest good ends: 60 - 15 - 10 = 35 minutes, more than half the hour. Break long lectures up [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

activities.title: True or false: practice and critique
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: During the practice session itself, blocked practice scores better than random practice.
cards.why: True. Blocked practice performance scores well during practice compared with random practice [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

cards.s: On a test the next day, blocked practice beats random practice.
cards.why: False. On a test the next day, random practice does better [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

cards.s: Early evaluation is mainly teacher oriented and checks teaching effectiveness.
cards.why: True. Early evaluation is usually teacher oriented and provides a check on teaching effectiveness [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

cards.s: A critique should wait until the next lesson so the learner can calm down.
cards.why: False. A critique should come immediately after the performance, while details are easy to recall [[25:141|AIH 6-10]].

cards.s: Overlearning can make a checklist recitation come apart from the thinking it should trigger.
cards.why: True. A checklist can become so automatic that the recitation is decoupled from the thoughts and actions it should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

cards.s: Deliberate practice works best with plenty of distractions mixed in.
cards.why: False. Learners achieve better results if distractions are avoided during deliberate practice [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].

activities.title: A landing lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI for Sam, a learner pilot with 22 hours who is working on landings in a four-seat high-wing trainer.

steps.s: Sam arrives straight from a night shift, yawning and short with the dispatcher.
options: Fly, but add extra landings to make up time
Switch to a short ground lesson or reschedule
Fly, and let him rest during cruise
steps.why: Irritability and inattention are signs of acute fatigue [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Fatigue is the primary consideration in lesson length, and instruction should go on only while the learner is alert and receptive [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

steps.s: Two lessons later, Sam's landings have been flat for three flights and he says he is 'just bad at this.'
options: Do 20 more touch-and-goes in a row
Explain plateaus are normal, work on another task, then return
Tell him he will fail the checkride if this continues
Say nothing and keep the same plan
steps.why: Explain the plateau is normal and temporary and move to a different place in the curriculum [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. More of the same drill can cause plateaus [[25:77|AIH 3-26]], and threats do not promote learning [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

steps.s: Today Sam is flying steep turns for the first time. You plan to drop a pencil as a distraction.
options: Do it on his first turn
Wait until he can fly the turn reasonably well alone
Do it, but only on the roll-out
steps.why: In the cognitive stage distractions make performance fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Individual tasks should be done reasonably well in isolation before you add more [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]; then distractions are a legitimate tool [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

steps.s: On the next approach Sam starts to round out a little high, with plenty of runway and no danger yet.
options: Let him go part way and find the way out, ready to take over
Ignore it and discuss it later
steps.why: Safety permitting, let learners go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Guard the controls and take over with 'I have the flight controls' if needed [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

steps.s: Back on the ground for the debrief.
options: Ask Sam to self-assess first, then compare and start with what went well
Skip it since it was a short flight
steps.why: Collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Positive comments on progress before areas to improve keep motivation up (law of effect) [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].
